citation: Kurz & Allison. Chicago In Early Days, 1779-1857. Chicago: Kurz & Allison, 76 & 78 Wabash Avenue, 1893. Chromolithograph, fifteen numbered vignettes with printed key.
author: Kurz & Allison
repository: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division; copy held in this repo at chicago/reference/photos/
locator: panel 14 (Sauganash Hotel); panel 11 (Green Tree); panel 5 (Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835); panel 9 (Wolf Point in 1830); panel 12 (The Old Kinzie Mansion, built 1832) — the panel this project's garden-fence layer reads, keyed at the foot of the sheet and numbered '12.' in the panel's own upper-left corner.
note:
Fifteen retrospective vignettes of early Chicago with a printed key giving names, build dates and populations. Panel 14, 'The Sauganash Hotel. Built in 1831', shows a two-story clapboard block with an attached single-story log wing and NO full-width gallery — the composition follows the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) closely enough that it is probably derived from it rather than an independent witness. Panel 5, 'Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835', is the most directly scene-relevant image in the sheet: picket palisade, a galleried barracks range, a blockhouse. Its own dating is unreliable — it puts the Kinzie Mansion at 1832, contradicting every documentary source.

PANEL 12 IS THE 'KINZIE-VIEW PLATE', AND THIS RECORD ALREADY HELD IT (T-0055). The plate the garden-fence layer has been citing by committed path since it was written — data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_1.png, 391 x 287 px, sha256 f796f89dbdc23a9a592bd722e9ddb0a55265efdbb55835a74fb0859fb17f6543, described in that directory's README as "the Kinzie mansion group (plate '12')" — is panel 12 of THIS sheet. It is a crop of it, and the project has held the whole sheet as a source since before the fence layer existed. So data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json's long-standing finding, 'this project holds NO source record for the Kinzie-view plate', was wrong in its conclusion while right about the symptom: the record was here and nothing joined it.

HOW THE JOIN WAS PROVED, rather than recognised. Three things agree and any one of them alone would be an eyeball. (a) The panel's own printed numeral: '12.' sits in the upper-left corner of p6_1 and in the upper-left corner of the sheet's lower-left vignette. (b) The printed key at the foot of the sheet, transcribed from the committed copy: "No. 12.  The Old Kinzie Mansion, built 1832.  Population 310." — the same 1832 build date this record's note already flags as unreliable, and the line immediately below "No. 11.  The Green Tree Hotel, cor. West Lake and Canal St.  Built in 1833.", whose panel is the set's OTHER numbered plate, p6_0, carrying '11.' in its own upper-right corner. (c) A normalised cross-correlation of p6_1 against the sheet (chicago/reference/photos/IMG_5382.png, 2048 x 1624): the best match over a scale sweep is 0.797 at 0.88x, at sheet pixels (94,1164)-(438,1416) — the lower-left vignette — against a best of 0.341 anywhere in the bird's-eye panel used as a control. The crop is the panel, at 88 % of the committed sheet's scale.

WHAT THAT CHANGES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The garden fence's evidence is not one grade stronger for being identified: this is still panel 12 of a chromolithograph published fifty-eight years after the scene date, it is still tier 5, and it still may never drive a coordinate. What changes is that the citation is now a source_id with a date, a publisher, an expired copyright and a holding institution instead of a path into an asset directory, and that the reader who wants to check the fence can reach the Library of Congress scan rather than a 391-px crop. Note the direction of the rights news: the fence layer had been reading a plate it recorded as unheld and therefore un-cleared, and the plate is public domain.

rights_note: The sheet carries its own copyright line at the foot, read off the committed copy verbatim: "Copyrighted 1893 by Kurz & Allison, 76 & 78 Wabash Avenue, Chicago, Ills." A US copyright first secured in 1893 has expired, which is why this record is public_domain rather than check_required, and it is the only plate in this project's pictorial set whose rights are settled ON THE OBJECT rather than by inference. The Library of Congress copy at the url carries no restriction of its own.
